rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate all eight compounds and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A moderate temperature leaves room to explore temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

Test a substantial temperature change at the same gradient to probe selectivity within the crowded middle cluster and the final pair. All peaks currently elute well before 10 minutes, leaving time headroom for later gradient adjustments.

Probe the low-temperature selectivity limit with the gradient unchanged. Comparing both temperature extremes will help distinguish persistent close pairs from temperature-induced crossings before adjusting gradient slope.

Retain the best temperature and flatten the gradient to test whether the two remaining critical pairs separate. The current last peak at 7.30 minutes provides room to improve resolution before incurring a substantial time penalty.
Use a shallower gradient to improve the remaining critical pair, while raising the starting organic fraction to offset the added retention time. Keep the temperature at the best-performing 25 C.
Flatten the gradient by one step to lift the sole remaining critical pair from R = 1.40 above 1.5. The last peak is expected to remain near or below 10 minutes, potentially achieving the maximum CRF.

The maximum CRF is already secured; now test a higher starting organic fraction and shorter gradient to reduce elution time while retaining full resolution. This keeps the gradient slope close to injection 6 while reducing the initial low-organic portion.

Increase gradient duration one step at the higher starting organic fraction to recover the critical pair’s resolution. This may preserve CRF 1.000 while eluting the final peak earlier than injection 6.

Test a higher starting organic fraction to shorten the elution window, compensating with a shallower gradient to protect the marginal critical pair. Injection 8 remains the fastest fully resolved method observed.

Test whether a modest temperature increase improves critical-pair selectivity enough to permit the shorter gradient from injection 7. This explores a faster route while retaining injection 8 as a fully resolved fallback.

Combine a higher starting organic fraction with a shallower gradient to balance the two critical middle pairs at 30 C. This tests whether full resolution can be recovered while keeping the last peak earlier than injection 8.

Lower the temperature one step to separate the final pair that limited injection 11. Relative to injection 9, the longer gradient should also improve the middle critical pair, potentially restoring full resolution near nine minutes.

With maximum CRF already secured, test a substantially faster, higher-organic gradient for an alternative selectivity regime. The critical middle pair has changed elution order as slope varies, so a steeper gradient may separate it on the other side of that crossing.

Raise the starting organic fraction one step to test whether the nearly resolved middle pair improves while shortening the elution window further. The slightly shallower slope may also preserve resolution of the late pair, currently at R = 1.59.
Shorten the fastest fully resolved method by one gradient-duration step to test the speed limit. Monitor the middle and late critical pairs, which have only modest resolution margins in injection 14.

Shortening the gradient compromised two pairs, so retain the 12-minute gradient and test temperature-driven selectivity for a faster separation. Injection 14 remains the fastest fully resolved fallback while this run probes a different elution-order regime.

Return to 25 C and test a higher starting organic fraction with a shallower gradient to protect the critical middle pair. This may shorten the elution window relative to injection 14 without sacrificing full resolution.

Test a single temperature step above the fastest fully resolved method to see whether elution can be accelerated without losing critical-pair resolution. The poor result at 45 C does not establish how selectivity behaves near 25 C.

Probe beyond the middle-pair convergence seen at higher starting organic fraction to test whether an elution-order reversal yields a faster resolved separation. Injection 14 remains the fastest confirmed method with maximum CRF.

Flatten the gradient at phi0 = 0.40 to test whether the sole critical pair from injection 17 can reach R ≥ 1.5. This brackets the resolution limit at the higher starting organic fraction while preserving injection 14 as the fastest fully resolved fallback.

Narrow the programmed gradient while preserving injection 14’s slope of 0.05 organic fraction per minute. Since all peaks eluted before either gradient ends, this should retain maximum CRF and the 4.14-minute elution window with a shorter gradient program.

Test a gradient slope midway between the fully resolved injection 21 and the faster but under-resolved injection 15. This refines the speed–resolution boundary while retaining the confirmed CRF 1.000 method as the fallback.

Test a modest temperature increase around the nearly fully resolved injection 13, whose middle-pair spacing differs from the phi0 = 0.35 methods. This may offer a faster fully resolved alternative; injection 14 remains the confirmed fallback.

Compress the gradient program to four minutes while preserving the successful slope of 0.05 organic fraction per minute. The gradient ends at the outlet at 4.65 minutes, after the confirmed last peak at 4.14 minutes, so full resolution and maximum CRF should be retained.

Test the minimum gradient duration at the successful initial slope, followed by a hold that may preserve late-pair resolution. Injection 24 remains the confirmed maximum-CRF fallback if the earlier hold broadens or delays the late peaks excessively.
